messages.author: 364b34b2b0ded261
messages.subject: phylogenetic 2B-PLS (phylo.integration) - strange result
parts:
Dear all,

I have a question on how to interpret the outcome of a phylogenetic 2B-PLS using the phylo.integration function.
Input is (1) a matrix containing shape coordinates for the distal ulna and (2) another matrix containing results on maximal range of motion of the wrist during ulnar deviation. I include a phylogenetic tree, and to match the tips of the tree (i.e. one datapoint per tip) the matrices above obviously contain mean shapes and mean range of motion.

When looking at the plot, I find it strange how the red regression line is drawn ... Judging from the datapoints, I would expect it to be more in between "Nomascus" and "Hylobates" on the right side, no? What does the analysis take into account to calculate this line?

Marie.

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] phylogenetic 2B-PLS (phylo.integration) - strange result
parts:
Dear Marie,

The line is a best-fit line based on least-squares.  It is not “drawn” to match any perception of how it should be drawn.  It is exactly what it is, the line that minimizes squared distances of points to it.

It appears that Pan paniscus has a lot of leverage.  You could remove this species, re-run the analysis, check the line as well as the r-PLS statistical results and if it appears everything improves in a way that heartens your perception, you know this species is something of an outlier, and investigation into why should be biologically interesting.  What is it about Pan paniscus that causes this species to have an association between ulna shape and function that bucks the trend you see in other primates?

It could also simply be that there is not much association between ulna shape and range of motion in the primates you sampled.  There does not have to be a pattern.

Best,

Mike

Hi Mike,

I have an additional question: when I run a regular 2B-PLS analysis, so without the phylogenetic context (no mean values), the correlation is strongly positive and significant for the ulna during supination (see figure attached, don't mind the annotation on the x-axis, is says triquetrum but that's my mistake). I also see the same trend for the triquetrum and hamate. Could you tell me why this is such a big difference compared to the plot of the analysis above? Is it because in the 2B-pPLS we take the phylogenetic relationship of the different primates into account?

Thanks!

Marie.

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] phylogenetic 2B-PLS (phylo.integration) - strange result
parts: Is it because in the 2B-pPLS we take the phylogenetic relationship of the different primates into account?

Yes.

One might say that the significant (not really positive even if the line looks like that) relationship when not taking phylogeny into account is spurious, because the observations are not independent.  The expectation is that species with more recent evolutionary divergence have more correlated shapes, so accounting for that auto-correlation in a PGLS analysis is why the result is less correlated.  An alternative explanation is that evolutionary divergence is constrained along an integrated axis of shape and function.  Anatomical changes that result in improper function are not likely to evolve.   Accounting for phylogeny in 2B-PLS might reveal the subtle, novel evolutionary directions species take, independent of the anatomical constraint.  In your data set, 2B-PLS done without phylogeny might reveal a strong shape-function association that permeates all species, and 2B-PLS, after accounting for that association, might reveal the more unique evolutionary divergences independent of the association.

Some published work here and here might help to elucidate more about what I am getting at, although these works are more focused on the morphological modules.  

Cheers!
Mike
